**Pattern.** Grid DFS / BFS flood fill

**Ask yourself.**

- What is a node and what is an edge here?
- How do I mark visited (in place or a set)?

**The leap.** Each unvisited land cell starts a flood fill that sinks the whole island; count the fills.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time: nested loops over m rows and n columns visit every cell, and each flood fill sinks a land cell at most once, so every cell is processed a constant number of times. O(m·n) space in the worst case: the DFS recursion or BFS queue can hold every cell when the grid is all land.

**Trap.** Recursion depth on large grids; diagonal adjacency.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-count-number-of-islands">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-course-schedule">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Course Schedule: 'prerequisites', 'can you finish all courses'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Topological sort / cycle detection in a directed graph

**Ask yourself.**

- Is this simply 'does the directed graph contain a cycle'?
- Three-colour DFS or Kahn's indegree queue?

**The leap.** A valid order exists iff there is no directed cycle: detect via DFS states (visiting/visited) or by checking that Kahn's algorithm processes every node.

**Complexity.** O(V + E) time: the DFS or Kahn's algorithm visits every course and every prerequisite edge once. O(V + E) space: the adjacency list of V lists and E edges, plus the state or in-degree array and the recursion stack or queue, each up to V.

**Trap.** A plain visited set cannot distinguish a back edge from a cross edge; reversed edge direction.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-course-schedule">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-pacific-atlantic-water-flow">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: 'water can flow to both oceans', heights, 'flows to equal or lower'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Multi-source reverse DFS / BFS from the borders

**Ask yourself.**

- Simulate from every cell, or reverse the flow from each ocean's border?
- Which comparison direction do I use when climbing?

**The leap.** Start from each ocean's border cells and climb to cells with height ≥ current; the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time: one reverse DFS or BFS per ocean from its border cells, each cell visited at most once per ocean, so 2·m·n steps. O(m·n) space: two visited grids of m·n cells plus the recursion stack or queue.

**Trap.** Forward simulation per cell (quadratic); reversing the height comparison incorrectly.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-pacific-atlantic-water-flow">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-valid-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Graph Valid Tree: 'n nodes and a list of edges', 'valid tree'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Union Find (or DFS) + edge count

**Ask yourself.**

- What two properties define a tree on n nodes?

**The leap.** Exactly n − 1 edges and fully connected (equivalently: connected and acyclic).

**Complexity.** O(n·α(n)) time: reject unless there are exactly n − 1 edges, then n − 1 unions each cost α(n) amortized, nearly constant, with path compression and union by rank. O(n) space: the parent and rank arrays.

**Trap.** Checking only connectivity or only the edge count; undirected DFS needs parent tracking to avoid false cycles.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-valid-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Greedy (2)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-jump-game">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Jump Game: 'can you reach the last index', 'maximum jump length'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Greedy farthest-reach

**Ask yourself.**

- What is the farthest index reachable so far?
- When exactly am I stuck?

**The leap.** Track the farthest reachable index; if the current index exceeds it, fail; or move the goal leftward from the end.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n indices, O(1) work each to update the farthest reach or the goal. O(1) space: only the farthest reachable index or the goal index.

**Trap.** Quadratic DP; confusing with the minimum-jumps variant.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-jump-game">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-maximum-subarray">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Maximum Subarray: 'maximum sum of a contiguous subarray'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Kadane's algorithm (greedy / DP)

**Ask yourself.**

- At each element: extend the current run or start fresh?
- When does a prefix stop being useful?

**The leap.** current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]); a negative running sum never helps.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n elements, O(1) work to extend or restart the running sum. O(1) space: the running sum and the best sum.

**Trap.** Initialising to 0 when all numbers may be negative.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-maximum-subarray">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Heap / Priority Queue (1)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-find-median-in-a-data-stream">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Find Median From Data Stream: 'stream', 'median at any time', 'addNum / findMedian'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two heaps (max-heap low half, min-heap high half)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which structure keeps the middle available after O(log n) insertions?
- How do I keep the two halves balanced?

**The leap.** Split the numbers into a lower half (max-heap) and upper half (min-heap) whose sizes differ by at most one; the median is at the tops.

**Complexity.** O(log n) time per insert: one push and at most one rebalancing move, each log n on a heap of up to n elements. O(1) time per median: it reads only the two heap tops. O(n) space: the two heaps together hold all n numbers.

**Trap.** Min-heap-only library (negate for the max-heap); rebalancing in the wrong direction.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-find-median-in-a-data-stream">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Intervals (5)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-insert-new-interval">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Insert Interval: 'sorted non-overlapping intervals', 'insert and merge if necessary'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Interval linear scan (three phases)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which intervals end before the new one, which overlap, which start after?

**The leap.** Append everything ending before; merge everything overlapping into the new interval; append the rest.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n already-sorted intervals, each appended or merged once. O(n) space: the output list of up to n + 1 intervals.

**Trap.** Wrong overlap condition; forgetting to append the new interval when it belongs at the end.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-insert-new-interval">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-meeting-schedule-ii">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Meeting Rooms II: 'minimum number of conference rooms'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sweep line (sorted starts and ends)

**Ask yourself.**

- How many meetings are in progress at any instant?
- Sort starts and ends separately, or keep a heap of end times?

**The leap.** Rooms = maximum concurrency: +1 at each start, −1 at each end (or the heap size after popping finished meetings).

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time: sorting costs n log n, then the sweep over the sorted starts and ends is one pass of n, or the heap version does up to n pushes and pops at log n each. O(n) space: the two sorted arrays or the heap of up to n meetings.

**Trap.** Tie order when a meeting ends exactly as another starts; reusing the Meeting Rooms logic.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-meeting-schedule-ii">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-meeting-schedule">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Meeting Rooms: 'can a person attend all meetings'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sort + adjacent overlap check

**Ask yourself.**

- After sorting by start, what must hold for every adjacent pair?

**The leap.** Any start earlier than the previous end is a conflict.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time: sorting by start costs n log n and dominates the single pass that compares each start with the previous end. O(1) space: only the previous end, when the sort is done in place.

**Trap.** Boundary semantics when one meeting ends exactly as another starts.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-meeting-schedule">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-intervals">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Merge Intervals: 'merge all overlapping intervals'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sort by start + sweep

**Ask yourself.**

- After sorting by start, when does the current interval overlap the last merged one?

**The leap.** If start ≤ last.end, extend last.end to the max; otherwise start a new interval.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time: sorting by start costs n log n and dominates the single pass that extends the last interval or appends a new one. O(n) space: the output list of up to n intervals.

**Trap.** Not taking the max of ends; inclusive vs exclusive touching.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-intervals">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-non-overlapping-intervals">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Non Overlapping Intervals: 'minimum number of intervals to remove'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Greedy by earliest end

**Ask yourself.**

- When two intervals overlap, which one should I keep?

**The leap.** Keep the interval that ends earliest (it leaves the most room); count the others as removals.

**Complexity.** O(n log n) time: sorting by end costs n log n and dominates the single pass that keeps the earliest end. O(1) space: one running end and a removal count, the sort's own space excluded.

**Trap.** Sorting by start and keeping the longer; not seeing the equivalence with maximum non-overlapping set.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-non-overlapping-intervals">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Linked List (6)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-linked-list-cycle-detection">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Linked List Cycle: 'cycle', 'constant memory'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Fast / slow pointers (Floyd)

**Ask yourself.**

- Why must a fast pointer meet a slow one inside a cycle?
- What null checks does the fast pointer need?

**The leap.** A pointer moving two steps gains one node per iteration on a pointer moving one; inside a cycle they must meet.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: the fast pointer reaches the end within n/2 steps when there is no cycle, and inside a cycle it gains one node per step, so it catches the slow pointer within one lap of at most n nodes. O(1) space: only the two pointers.

**Trap.** Missing fast.next null checks; using a set when O(1) space was expected.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-linked-list-cycle-detection">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-k-sorted-linked-lists">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Merge K Sorted Lists: 'k sorted lists', 'merge all'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Heap (k-way merge)

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I pick the global minimum among k heads cheaply?
- Does pairwise merging in log k rounds give the same complexity?

**The leap.** A min-heap over the k current heads yields the next element in O(log k); or merge lists in pairs, halving the count each round.

**Complexity.** O(N log k) time with a heap: N total nodes, each pushed and popped once, log k on a heap of size k. O(k) space: the heap holds one head per list. Pairwise merging is also O(N log k) time: log k rounds, each touching all N nodes once. O(1) space: nodes are spliced iteratively, with no heap.

**Trap.** Sequential merging is O(N·k); heap tuples need an index tie-breaker because nodes are not comparable.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-k-sorted-linked-lists">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-merge-two-sorted-linked-lists">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Merge Two Sorted Lists: 'two sorted linked lists', 'merge into one sorted list'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two-pointer merge with dummy head

**Ask yourself.**

- Does a dummy head remove the head special case?
- What happens to the remainder of the longer list?

**The leap.** Splice existing nodes by comparison behind a dummy head; attach the leftover tail.

**Complexity.** O(n + m) time: one pass over both lists, each node spliced once. O(1) space: only the dummy head and the tail pointer, because existing nodes are reused.

**Trap.** Allocating new nodes; forgetting the leftover tail.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-merge-two-sorted-linked-lists">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-remove-node-from-end-of-linked-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Remove Nth Node From End of List: 'nth node from the end', 'one pass'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two pointers with a fixed gap

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I place one pointer n steps ahead of another?
- What if the node to remove is the head?

**The leap.** Start a lead pointer n+1 ahead from a dummy; when it reaches the end, the trailing pointer is just before the target.

**Complexity.** O(L) time: one pass over the list's L nodes, with the lead pointer kept n + 1 nodes ahead of the trailing one. O(1) space: two pointers and a dummy head.

**Trap.** Removing the head without a dummy; off-by-one in the gap.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-remove-node-from-end-of-linked-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-reorder-linked-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Reorder List: 'L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 …', 'in place'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Linked List composition (middle → reverse → interleave)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which known primitives compose here?
- Where do I cut the first half so no cycle forms?

**The leap.** Find the middle with slow/fast, reverse the second half, then interleave the two halves.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: three passes, finding the middle, reversing the second half, then merging, each over at most n nodes. O(1) space: a few pointers, because nodes are relinked in place.

**Trap.** Not terminating the first half; odd/even middle handling.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-reorder-linked-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-reverse-a-linked-list">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Reverse Linked List: 'reverse', singly linked list, 'iteratively and recursively'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Linked List pointer manipulation

**Ask yourself.**

- Which three pointers do I need, and which must be saved first?
- What does the recursive version return?

**The leap.** prev / cur / next: save next, point cur.next at prev, advance.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n nodes, each pointer flipped once. O(1) space iteratively: only the prev, cur and next pointers. O(n) space recursively: one stack frame per node.

**Trap.** Overwriting .next before saving it.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-reverse-a-linked-list">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Math & Geometry (3)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-rotate-matrix">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Rotate Image: 'rotate 90 degrees clockwise in place'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Matrix in-place transform (transpose + reverse)

**Ask yourself.**

- Can the rotation decompose into simpler in-place operations?

**The leap.** Transpose, then reverse each row (clockwise).

**Complexity.** O(n²) time: transpose then reverse each row, each of the n² cells swapped a constant number of times. O(1) space: swaps happen in place.

**Trap.** Layer-by-layer index errors; rotating the wrong way.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-rotate-matrix">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-set-zeroes-in-matrix">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Set Matrix Zeroes: 'set entire row and column to zero', 'O(1) space'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** In-place marking with first row / column

**Ask yourself.**

- Where can I store per-row and per-column flags without extra memory?
- How do I protect the marker row/column's own state?

**The leap.** Use the first row and first column as flag storage plus one extra variable for their own status; apply zeroes afterwards in the right order.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time: one pass over the m·n cells to mark zeros in the first row and column, then one pass to apply them. O(1) space: the first row and column act as the markers, plus one extra flag for their own status.

**Trap.** Overwriting markers before reading them; zeroing the first row/column too early.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-set-zeroes-in-matrix">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-spiral-matrix">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Spiral Matrix: 'spiral order'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Boundary-pointer traversal

**Ask yourself.**

- What four boundaries shrink after each pass?
- When must I stop early to avoid visiting cells twice?

**The leap.** Maintain top/bottom/left/right; traverse four edges, shrink, and re-check bounds before the bottom and left passes.

**Complexity.** O(m·n) time: every cell visited once while four boundaries shrink inward. O(1) space: four boundary indices, the output excluded.

**Trap.** Double-visiting on a leftover single row or column.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-spiral-matrix">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Sliding Window (4)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-buy-and-sell-crypto">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Best Time to Buy And Sell Stock: 'buy one day, sell a later day', 'maximum profit', single transaction</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sliding window / running minimum

**Ask yourself.**

- For each day, what is the best day to have bought before it?
- Is this a running minimum plus a running best?

**The leap.** Track the minimum price so far; profit at day i is price − min so far; keep the best.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n prices, O(1) work per day. O(1) space: only the minimum price so far and the best profit.

**Trap.** Allowing a sale before the purchase; nested loops.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-buy-and-sell-crypto">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-repeating-substring-with-replacement">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Repeating Character Replacement: 'replace at most k characters', 'longest substring with the same letter'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sliding Window + max frequency

**Ask yourself.**

- When is a window fixable with k replacements? (length − most frequent ≤ k)
- Does the max frequency need to decrease when the window shrinks?

**The leap.** A window is valid iff its length minus its most frequent count is ≤ k; the historical max frequency never needs decrementing to get the right answer.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: each character enters and leaves the window at most once, with O(1) per count update and max check. O(26) space: one count per uppercase letter.

**Trap.** Recomputing the max on every step (acceptable at 26) or shrinking the window incorrectly.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-repeating-substring-with-replacement">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-longest-substring-without-duplicates">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters: 'longest substring', 'without repeating characters'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sliding Window (variable) + last-seen map

**Ask yourself.**

- What makes the window valid, and can I check it in O(1)?
- When a repeat enters, how far must the left edge jump?

**The leap.** Maintain a window of unique characters; on a repeat, move left just past the previous occurrence (never backwards).

**Complexity.** O(n) time: each character enters the window once and the left pointer only moves forward, so each leaves at most once, with O(1) average per hash map lookup. O(alphabet) space: the hash map holds at most one last-seen index per distinct character.

**Trap.** Moving left by one instead of jumping; forgetting max(left, last_seen + 1).

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-longest-substring-without-duplicates">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-minimum-window-with-characters">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Minimum Window Substring: 'minimum window of s containing every character of t', counts matter, 'hard'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sliding Window (need/have counters)

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I know in O(1) that the window satisfies t? (a formed/satisfied counter)
- Expand until formed, then shrink while still formed — what updates on each move?

**The leap.** Track need counts vs have counts and the number of fully satisfied characters; expand right until satisfied, shrink left while satisfied, record the smallest.

**Complexity.** O(|s| + |t|) time: one pass over t builds the need counts, then each character of s enters and leaves the window at most once, with O(1) average per hash map update. O(alphabet) space: the need and have maps hold at most one count per distinct character.

**Trap.** Mishandling duplicate characters in t; recording the answer before the window is fully formed.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-minimum-window-with-characters">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Stack (1)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-validate-parentheses">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Valid Parentheses: 'brackets', 'valid/balanced', 'closed in the correct order'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Stack (matching)

**Ask yourself.**

- What must the most recent unmatched opener be when a closer arrives?
- What is left on the stack at the end?

**The leap.** LIFO matching: push openers, pop and compare on closers; the stack must be empty at the end.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one pass over n characters, each bracket pushed and popped at most once. O(n) space: the stack, up to n opening brackets.

**Trap.** Popping an empty stack; forgetting leftover openers.

</details>

## Recognition: Trees (11)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder-traversal">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Construct Binary Tree From Preorder And Inorder Traversal: 'preorder and inorder', 'construct the tree'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Divide & conquer on traversal arrays

**Ask yourself.**

- What does the first preorder element tell me?
- How does that element's position in inorder split left and right subtree sizes?

**The leap.** Preorder gives the root; its index in inorder gives the left size; recurse on the corresponding ranges using an index map.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: every node is created once, and the value-to-index map makes each inorder lookup O(1) average. With linear searches instead, each of n nodes scans up to n inorder entries, so O(n²). O(n) space: the value-to-index map holds n entries, plus the recursion depth h, n when skewed.

**Trap.** Slicing arrays (hidden O(n²) copies); wrong preorder offset for the right subtree.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-binary-tree-from-preorder-and-inorder-traversal">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-binary-tree-maximum-path-sum">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum: 'path between any two nodes', 'maximum sum', negative values present, 'hard'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS post-order with two meanings

**Ask yourself.**

- What does a subtree hand upward (one branch) versus what does it record globally (both branches)?
- What do I do with negative contributions?

**The leap.** Return the best single-branch gain (floored at zero) to the parent while updating a global best with left + right + node.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one post-order traversal visits every node once and does O(1) work there. O(h) space: the recursion depth, the height h, log n when balanced and n when skewed.

**Trap.** Passing both branches upward; not clamping negatives.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-binary-tree-maximum-path-sum">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-depth-of-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Maximum Depth of Binary Tree: 'maximum depth', 'longest root-to-leaf path'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS (post-order height)

**Ask yourself.**

- What single number does each subtree return to its parent?

**The leap.** height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)).

**Complexity.** O(n) time: every node is visited once with O(1) work. O(h) space: the recursion depth, the height h, log n when balanced and n when skewed.

**Trap.** Counting edges vs nodes; recursion depth on skewed trees.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-depth-of-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-invert-a-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Invert Binary Tree: 'invert', 'mirror', 'swap left and right'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS (local swap)

**Ask yourself.**

- Is the operation purely local to each node?

**The leap.** Swap the children at each node and recurse; any traversal order works.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: every node is visited once and its two children swapped in O(1). O(h) space: the recursion depth, the height h, log n when balanced and n when skewed.

**Trap.** None serious — this is a warm-up to make recursion automatic.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-invert-a-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-kth-smallest-integer-in-bst">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Kth Smallest Element In a Bst: 'kth smallest', 'BST'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** BST inorder traversal (iterative, early stop)

**Ask yourself.**

- What order does inorder produce?
- Can I stop after k nodes instead of traversing everything?

**The leap.** Inorder of a BST is sorted; an explicit stack lets you stop at the kth visit.

**Complexity.** O(h + k) time: every node pushed on the stack is either popped as one of the k visits or still waiting on the stack, which holds at most h, so at most h + k pushes and pops. O(h) space: the explicit stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path, log n when balanced and n when skewed.

**Trap.** Collecting the whole inorder list (correct but O(n)); off-by-one on k.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-kth-smallest-integer-in-bst">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-level-order-traversal-of-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Binary Tree Level Order Traversal: 'level order', 'return values per level'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree BFS (level by level)

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I know where one level ends inside the queue?

**The leap.** Process exactly len(queue) nodes per round; each round is one level.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: every node is enqueued and dequeued once. O(w) space: the queue holds at most one level, the widest level w, up to about n/2 in a full tree, output excluded.

**Trap.** Not snapshotting the queue size before the inner loop.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-level-order-traversal-of-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-lowest-common-ancestor-in-binary-search-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree: 'lowest common ancestor', 'BST'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** BST property walk

**Ask yourself.**

- How does the ordering tell me whether both nodes lie left, right, or split?

**The leap.** Walk down from the root: both smaller → left, both larger → right, otherwise the current node is the split point.

**Complexity.** O(h) time: one step down per level, the height h, log n when balanced and n when skewed. O(1) space iteratively: only the current node pointer, while a recursive walk would use O(h) for the call stack.

**Trap.** Using the general-tree LCA algorithm (works but ignores the property); forgetting a node can be its own ancestor.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-lowest-common-ancestor-in-binary-search-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-same-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Same Tree: 'structurally identical and same values'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS (lockstep traversal)

**Ask yourself.**

- What are the base cases when one or both nodes are null?

**The leap.** Recurse on both trees simultaneously; equality of structure and value at every node.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one paired DFS, every node of both trees visited once. O(h) space: the recursion depth, the height h, log n when balanced, n when skewed.

**Trap.** Comparing values before null checks.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-same-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Serialize And Deserialize Binary Tree: 'serialize / deserialize', 'any binary tree', 'design'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS preorder with null markers

**Ask yourself.**

- How do I mark missing children so the structure is unambiguous?
- Which traversal is easiest to invert with a token iterator?

**The leap.** Preorder with explicit null markers is self-delimiting; deserialisation consumes tokens in the same order.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: every node visited once to serialize and once to rebuild. O(n) space: the serialized string with one token per node and null marker, plus the recursion depth.

**Trap.** Delimiters versus multi-digit or negative values; recursion depth.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-subtree-of-a-binary-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Subtree of Another Tree: 'subRoot is a subtree of root', 'same structure and values'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS with Same Tree as a helper

**Ask yourself.**

- Where could a match start?
- Can I reuse Same Tree at every candidate node?

**The leap.** At each node of the big tree, test identity against subRoot with the Same Tree check.

**Complexity.** O(n·m) time: each of the n nodes of the big tree may start a Same Tree check that walks up to m nodes. O(h) space: the recursion depth of the big tree. Serialising both trees and matching strings gives O(n + m) time: each tree is serialised once, then a linear-time matcher such as KMP scans the two strings once. O(n + m) space: the two serialised strings.

**Trap.** Accepting a partial match; forgetting the empty-subtree edge semantics.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-subtree-of-a-binary-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-valid-binary-search-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Validate Binary Search Tree: 'valid BST', 'left subtree only smaller, right subtree only larger'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Tree DFS with propagated bounds

**Ask yourself.**

- Is checking against immediate children enough? (no)
- What bounds does each node inherit from its ancestors?

**The leap.** Every node must lie strictly inside an (low, high) interval inherited from above; or the inorder sequence must be strictly increasing.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: one DFS visiting every node once, checking it against the bounds passed down. O(h) space: the recursion depth, log n when balanced, n when skewed.

**Trap.** Comparing only with children; equal values; sentinel handling for the bounds.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-valid-binary-search-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Tries (3)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-design-word-search-data-structure">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Design Add And Search Words Data Structure: 'search with '.' matching any letter'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Trie + DFS for wildcards

**Ask yourself.**

- What must happen at a '.' character?
- Where does the end-of-word check happen?

**The leap.** Walk the trie; on a wildcard, branch into every child (backtracking over the trie).

**Complexity.** O(26^dots · L) time per search in the worst case: each wildcard branches into up to 26 children, so dots wildcards give up to 26^dots paths, each walked at most L characters deep. O(total characters) space: the trie stores at most one node per inserted character.

**Trap.** Returning only the first child's result; ignoring the end flag at the last character.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-design-word-search-data-structure">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-implement-prefix-tree">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Implement Trie Prefix Tree: 'insert / search / startsWith', 'prefix tree'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Trie

**Ask yourself.**

- What does a node store?
- How is end-of-word distinguished from a prefix?

**The leap.** Children map per node plus an end flag; every operation walks one character per level.

**Complexity.** O(L) time per operation: insert, search and startsWith each walk one trie level per character of the length-L word, with O(1) average per child map lookup. O(total characters) space: the trie stores at most one node per inserted character, fewer when prefixes are shared.

**Trap.** Returning true from search when only a prefix exists; conflating search and startsWith.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-implement-prefix-tree">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-search-for-word-ii">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · HARD</span><span class="rev-q">Word Search II: 'find all words from a list in the grid', 'hard'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Trie + grid backtracking with pruning

**Ask yourself.**

- Why does running Word Search per word explode?
- How can a trie prune the grid DFS?

**The leap.** Build a trie of the words and DFS the grid while walking the trie simultaneously; stop at dead nodes, collect at word ends, and prune found words.

**Complexity.** O(m·n·4·3^(L−1)) time in the worst case, far less with pruning: m·n starting cells, 4 directions on the first step, then 3 per step for L − 1 more steps, where L is the longest word length, while the trie cuts dead prefixes early. O(total characters) space: one trie node per character across all words, plus the recursion depth L.

**Trap.** Duplicate results; not pruning found words or dead leaves (time limit); forgetting to unmark cells.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-search-for-word-ii">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

## Recognition: Two Pointers (3)

<p class="rev-plan">One card per problem: the name and its cues on the question side. Say the pattern, the key leap and the complexity, then open. Mark known only when all three came without thinking.</p>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-is-palindrome">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · EASY</span><span class="rev-q">Valid Palindrome: 'reads the same forward and backward', 'ignore non-alphanumeric', 'case-insensitive'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two Pointers (converging)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which characters count, and can I skip the others in place?
- Do I need to build a cleaned string at all?

**The leap.** Converge from both ends, skipping invalid characters, comparing normalised characters.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: two pointers move inward, so each character is visited at most once. O(1) space: only the two indices.

**Trap.** Allocating a filtered copy (fine, but O(n) space); mishandling the skip loop bounds.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-is-palindrome">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-max-water-container">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">Container With Most Water: 'two lines form a container', 'most water', heights array</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Two Pointers (greedy shrink)

**Ask yourself.**

- Which side limits the area — the shorter line or the taller?
- Why can moving the taller side never increase the area?

**The leap.** Area is bounded by the shorter line; moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can improve the result.

**Complexity.** O(n) time: the two pointers start at the ends and one moves inward each step, so n − 1 steps in total. O(1) space: only the two indices and the best area.

**Trap.** Brute-force pairs; moving the taller pointer.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-max-water-container">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>

<details class="rev" data-card="rec-three-integer-sum">
<summary><span class="rev-head"><span class="rev-tag">RECOGNITION · MEDIUM</span><span class="rev-q">3Sum: 'triplets that sum to zero', 'no duplicate triplets'</span></span></summary>
<div class="rev-a">

**Pattern.** Sort + two pointers

**Ask yourself.**

- After sorting and fixing one element, is this Two Sum on a sorted array?
- Where exactly do duplicates get skipped (anchor level and pointer level)?

**The leap.** Sort; for each anchor, converge two pointers on the remainder; skip equal neighbours at every level to avoid duplicate triplets.

**Complexity.** O(n²) time: sorting costs n log n, then each of the n anchors runs a two-pointer pass of up to n, which dominates. O(1) extra space: the pointers only, ignoring the output and the sort's own space.

**Trap.** Forgetting to move both pointers after a hit; skipping duplicates only at the anchor.

<p class="rev-actions"><button type="button" class="rev-known" data-for="rec-three-integer-sum">mark known</button></p>

</div>
</details>
